title: G2N2: Weisfeiler and Lehman Go Grammatical

en.text: The standard ruler for how much a graph neural network (GNN) can tell apart is the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) hierarchy: if two non-isomorphic graphs already look identical to the k-th-order WL test, no GNN in that class will separate them either. For years the field has worked in one direction only. You design a model on intuition, then go back and prove it matches, say, the third-order test. The expressiveness guarantee always arrives afterward, as a separate proof stapled onto the architecture.

The trouble is that there is no general recipe for that. Every new architecture needs its own bespoke expressiveness proof, and the reverse direction, starting from a mathematical object whose power you already know and mechanically building a network that inherits it, has been missing. Existing 3-WL models each pay a price: 3-IGN's operator basis grows like the 2k-th Bell number and is memory-hungry, while PPGN is tractable but was only shown to mimic 2-FWL, with no constructive bridge from a language to the model.

This ICLR 2024 paper, G2N2, runs the process the other way. Instead of "design first, prove later," it picks a language fragment whose expressiveness is already known, then reads the network's layers straight off that fragment's rules. The whole pipeline is automatic, the resulting network is provably 3-WL, and in practice it turns out faster and more accurate than the existing 3-WL models. The figure below is the whole paper in one picture.

en.caption: Figure 1. The full G2N2 derivation pipeline. Starting from the matrix-language fragment ML(L3), which is equivalent in power to the 3-WL test, the authors write an exhaustive context-free grammar G(L3), reduce it to the compact r-G(L3), and then read a G2N2 layer directly off the reduced grammar: surviving variables become the network's inputs and production rules become the layer's operations.

en.text: Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.01590    Code: https://github.com/JPiquenot/Wesfeiler-and-Lehman-go-grammatical
Background: from the WL hierarchy to a matrix language

The idea grows from a clean observation: the 1-WL and 3-WL tests can each be rewritten as a fragment of a matrix language called MATLANG. Concretely, two graphs are indistinguishable to 3-WL exactly when every "sentence" you can write in the fragment ML(L3) evaluates to the same value on both. That is a genuine bridge between combinatorics (the WL test) and linear algebra (matrix operations).

But a bridge is not yet a road. Turning such a fragment into an actual trainable network had only ever been done case by case, and the resulting models could rarely claim the full 3-WL guarantee. GNNML3, derived from the same MATLANG view, was shown to be more expressive than 1-WL but never proven to reach 3-WL, precisely because there was no systematic derivation. G2N2's goal is to pave that road once and for all.
Step one: from a language to a grammar, then to a reduced grammar

The derivation begins from a set of operations: L3 = {· (matrix product), ᵀ (transpose), 1 (the all-ones vector), diag (take the diagonal), ⊙ (element-wise product)}. The authors first write an exhaustive context-free grammar G(L3) whose generated sentences are exactly the fragment ML(L3). This step turns "a language" into "a set of production rules."

Then comes the key move: reduction. While proving at every step that no 3-WL expressiveness is lost, they strip away redundant rules and variables until only the essential core productions remain: the reduced grammar r-G(L3). Reduction both makes the eventual network leaner and, as a bonus, reveals which operations actually matter. To see how a rule becomes a computation, look at one iteration of the procedure below.

en.caption: Figure 2. One iteration in four steps. (1) Rule selection: pick a production from (M⊙M), (MM), diag(Vc), (MVc). (2) Input selection: fetch the operands that rule needs from the matrix memory and vector memory. (3) Rule computation: apply the operation (here, A⊙A²). (4) Output storage: write the result back into the matching memory. Iterating this loop gradually accumulates richer graph features in memory.

en.text: Step two: read the grammar rules as network layers

Once the reduced grammar is in hand, the network is almost literally read off it: the surviving variables tell you what the inputs should be (a tensor of node and edge features), and each surviving production rule becomes a piece of a layer. That correspondence is where the name G2N2, Grammatical Graph Neural Network, comes from.

A layer maintains two memories: an edge (matrix) memory C and a node (vector) memory H. Learnable linear blocks L1 through L7 combine slices of these tensors, the reduced rules (M⊙M), (MM), diag(Vc), and (MVc) are computed on top of them, and two MLPs, MLP_M and MLP_Vc, concatenate and merge the pieces into the next layer's C and H. The figure below unpacks the data flow inside one layer.

en.caption: Figure 4. Inside a single G2N2 layer. The edge tensor C and node tensor H enter on the left; L1–L5 linearly combine slices of C and take pairwise products following the rules (MM) and (M⊙M), while L6–L7 process H and turn it into diagonal matrices via diag. These intermediates, together with the inputs, feed MLP_M to produce the new edge tensor C^(l+1) and MLP_Vc to produce the new node tensor H^(l+1).

en.text: Stack k such layers, cap them with permutation-equivariant readout functions, and a complete G2N2 takes shape. The readouts act separately on the node memory H and on the diagonal and off-diagonal elements of the edge memory C, and a final decision layer turns their outputs into a prediction. The overall architecture looks like this.

en.caption: Figure 5. The full G2N2 architecture, graph to output. The input node and edge embeddings are updated by k stacked G2N2 layers; readout functions are then applied independently to H^(k) and to the diagonal and off-diagonal parts of C^(k), and a decision layer produces the final prediction.

en.text: Does it work? QM9 molecular regression

Beyond the theory, G2N2 holds up empirically. The first arena is QM9: roughly 130K small molecules with 12 quantum-chemical regression targets, of which R² is widely regarded as the hardest to predict. Trained one target at a time, G2N2 achieves the lowest MAE on all 12 targets while also running faster per epoch (98 seconds versus PPGN's 129). The most dramatic case is R²: the error drops from PPGN's 3.78 to 0.342, roughly an 11-fold improvement, and when all 12 targets are learned jointly, the gap widens further (16.07 versus 1.19).

en.caption: Table 1. Selected QM9 single-target regression results (MAE, lower is better) plus mean per-epoch time. Full results for all 12 targets are in the paper's Table 4.

en.text: Classification and a spectral stress test

The second arena is the classic TUD graph-classification benchmark, spanning molecular graphs like MUTAG and PTC and social graphs like IMDB. G2N2 beats the second-best GNN competitor on five of the six datasets, and ranks first outright on MUTAG, PTC, and Proteins.

en.caption: Table 2. TUD results comparing G2N2 with the strongest GNN competitor (accuracy, higher is better; G2N2's rank among GNNs in parentheses). Full results are in the paper's Table 6.

en.text: The third arena is closer to a stress test: learning spectral filters on 900-node graphs. Message-passing networks are known to behave like low-pass filters by default, so high-pass and especially band-pass filtering is where expressiveness really shows. The result is telling. PPGN nearly maxes out low-pass and high-pass but collapses on band-pass (R² of just 0.1041), whereas G2N2 stays strong across all three, reaching a band-pass R² of 0.8206. The authors argue PPGN fails here precisely because it lacks the kind of explicit edge memory that G2N2 keeps.

en.caption: Table 3. R² on spectral node regression (median of 10 runs, higher is better). PPGN fails on band-pass filtering; G2N2 remains robust across all three filter types.

en.text: Which rules matter: the grammar-reduction ablation

The experiment that best captures the method's flavor is the ablation around grammar reduction. On the QM9 R² target, the authors compare the full grammar G(L3), an intermediate grammar i-G(L3), and the reduced grammar r-G(L3): their errors are essentially the same, confirming that reduction only removes redundancy and leaves expressiveness untouched. But once you push past the reduced grammar and start deleting core rules, the error climbs noticeably.

That degradation is itself useful information: it quantifies how much each operation contributes to the final accuracy. In other words, when a task does not actually need the full 3-WL power, this plot tells you which rules you can safely drop, so you can prune the model deliberately instead of hacking away at parameters and hoping accuracy survives.

en.caption: Figure 6. Parameter count versus MAE on QM9's R² target. The full grammar G(L3), the intermediate i-G(L3), the reduced r-G(L3), and a variant adding one rule (Mᵀ) all land at comparable error; removing core rules such as {MM}, {M⊙M}, or diag(Vc) from r-G(L3) (marked with \) drives MAE up, confirming each rule pulls its weight.

en.text: Takeaway: expressiveness by construction

What G2N2 really changes is the workflow. Instead of designing a network and then hoping to prove it is expressive enough, you start from a language whose power you already know, reduce it to a clean grammar, and read the network directly off the rules, with expressiveness guaranteed by construction. The concrete payoff is a provably 3-WL model that is also faster and more accurate than its predecessors.

The more interesting point is that the "grammatical" framework is generic. In principle, any fragment of an algebraic language could be sent down the same route and turned into a network that inherits its expressive power. G2N2 is the first concrete instance of that idea, and it points toward a whole family of GNN designs where you choose the expressiveness you want up front and build the model to match.

zh.text: 衡量一个图神经网络（GNN）到底有多「聪明」，业界最常用的标尺是 Weisfeiler-Lehman（WL）层级：如果两张不同构的图连 k 阶 WL 测试都分不开，那么再强的 GNN 也分不开。于是多年来的惯例是,先凭直觉设计一个模型,再回过头去证明它能匹配某一阶 WL 测试。表达力的保证,总是作为「事后」的一纸证明补上来的。
问题在于,这条路没有通用配方。每设计一个新架构,就要重新写一遍表达力证明;而反过来的方向,也就是「给定一个已知表达力的数学片段,机械地造出一个继承其表达力的网络」,一直没有系统方法。已有的 3-WL 模型也各有短板:3-IGN 的算子基规模随 2k 阶 Bell 数爆炸,内存吃紧;PPGN 虽然可算,却只被证明能模拟 2-FWL,与语言表达力之间没有构造性的桥梁。
ICLR 2024 上的这篇 G2N2 反其道而行:它不再「先设计后证明」,而是「先选定一个表达力已知的语言片段,再把它的规则直接读成网络的层」。整条流水线是自动的,产出的网络可证明达到 3-WL 表达力,而且在实验里比现有 3-WL 模型更快、更准。下图是全文的一张总览。

zh.caption: 图1 G2N2 的整条推导流水线。从与 3-WL 等价的矩阵语言片段 ML(L3) 出发,先写出穷尽的上下文无关文法 G(L3),再约简为紧凑的 r-G(L3),最后把约简文法里存活下来的变量当作网络输入、产生式规则当作层内运算,直接得到 G2N2 的一层。

zh.text: 论文：https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.01590　　代码：https://github.com/JPiquenot/Wesfeiler-and-Lehman-go-grammatical
背景:从 WL 层级到矩阵语言
这套方法的起点,是一个漂亮的观察:1-WL 与 3-WL 测试都可以改写成一种矩阵语言 MATLANG 的片段。具体地说,两张图在 3-WL 看来一样,当且仅当片段 ML(L3) 里你能写出的每一个「句子」在两张图上取值都相同。这在组合数学(WL 测试)和线性代数(矩阵运算)之间架起了一座桥。
但桥不等于路。把这样一个片段变成真正可训练的网络,此前只能一个个手工来做,得到的模型往往拿不到完整的 3-WL 保证。例如同样从 MATLANG 视角出发的 GNNML3,只被证明比 1-WL 更强,而没能证到 3-WL,原因恰恰是缺少一条系统化的推导路径。G2N2 要做的,就是把这条路一次性铺好。
第一步:从语言到文法,再到约简文法
推导从一组算子开始:L3 = {·（矩阵乘）, ᵀ（转置）, 1（全一向量）, diag（取对角）, ⊙（逐元素乘）}。作者先写出一部穷尽的上下文无关文法 G(L3),它生成的句子恰好就是片段 ML(L3)。这一步把「一个语言」变成了「一组产生式规则」。
接着是关键的约简:在保证每一步都不损失 3-WL 表达力的前提下,不断删去冗余的规则和变量,直到只剩下最精简的核心产生式 r-G(L3)。约简既让后续的网络更轻,也顺带暴露出「哪些运算真正重要」。要理解规则如何变成计算,可以看下面这张一次迭代的示意图。

zh.caption: 图2 一次迭代的四个步骤。(1) 规则选择:从 (M⊙M)、(MM)、diag(Vc)、(MVc) 中挑一条产生式;(2) 输入选择:按所选规则从矩阵记忆和向量记忆里取出对应的输入;(3) 规则计算:执行该运算(图中为 A⊙A²);(4) 输出存储:把结果写回相应的记忆。逐次迭代,记忆里就积累出越来越丰富的图特征。

zh.text: 第二步:把文法规则读成网络的层
约简文法一旦到手,网络几乎是「读」出来的:存活下来的变量告诉你网络的输入该是什么(一组刻画节点与边的特征张量),而每一条存活的产生式规则,都对应层里的一块运算。这正是 G2N2(Grammatical Graph Neural Network)名字的由来。
一层内部维护两份记忆:边(矩阵)记忆 C 和节点(向量)记忆 H。可学习的线性块 L1 到 L7 负责组合张量的各个切片,约简后的规则 (M⊙M)、(MM)、diag(Vc)、(MVc) 在其上计算,再由两个多层感知机 MLP_M 与 MLP_Vc 把结果拼接、融合,分别输出下一层的 C 和 H。下图把这一层的数据流拆开来看。

zh.caption: 图4 G2N2 一层的内部结构。左侧输入边张量 C 与节点张量 H;L1–L5 线性组合 C 的切片并按规则 (MM)、(M⊙M) 做两两乘积,L6–L7 处理 H 并经 diag 化为对角矩阵;这些中间量连同输入一起送入 MLP_M 得到新的边张量 C^(l+1),送入 MLP_Vc 得到新的节点张量 H^(l+1)。

zh.text: 把这样的层堆叠 k 次,再在最后接上排列等变(permutation-equivariant)的读出函数,一个完整的 G2N2 就成形了。读出分别作用在节点记忆 H、以及边记忆 C 的对角与非对角元素上,最后交给决策层给出预测。整体架构如下。

zh.caption: 图5 G2N2 从图到输出的完整架构。输入的节点与边嵌入依次经过 k 个 G2N2 层不断更新;随后对 H^(k)、以及 C^(k) 的对角与非对角部分分别做读出,汇入决策层输出最终预测。

zh.text: 效果:QM9 分子回归

理论漂亮之外,G2N2 在实验上也站得住脚。第一个战场是 QM9:约 130K 个小分子、12 个量子化学回归目标,其中 R² 是公认最难预测的一项。逐个目标单独训练时,G2N2 在全部 12 个目标上都取得了最低的 MAE,同时每个 epoch 的训练还更快(98 秒对 PPGN 的 129 秒)。最戏剧性的是 R² 目标:误差从 PPGN 的 3.78 降到 0.342,约 11 倍的改善;而当 12 个目标一起训练时,两者的差距还会进一步拉大(16.07 对 1.19),可见约束越强,G2N2 的表达力优势越明显。

zh.caption: 表1 QM9 单目标回归的部分结果(指标为 MAE,越低越好),以及每 epoch 平均耗时。完整 12 个目标见论文表 4。

zh.text: 分类与一次频谱压力测试
第二个战场是经典的 TUD 图分类基准,从 MUTAG、PTC 这类分子图到 IMDB 这类社交图。G2N2 在其中 5 个数据集上都优于第二名的 GNN 竞争者,并在 MUTAG、PTC、Proteins 上直接排名第一。

zh.caption: 表2 TUD 数据集上 G2N2 与最强 GNN 竞争者的对比(指标为准确率,越高越好;括号内为 G2N2 在 GNN 中的排名)。完整结果见论文表 6。

zh.text: 第三个战场更像一次「压力测试」:在 900 节点大图上学习频谱滤波器。已知消息传递网络天然偏向低通滤波,而高通、带通滤波才是真正考验表达力的地方。结果颇能说明问题:PPGN 在低通、高通上都接近满分,却在带通上崩溃(R² 仅 0.1041);G2N2 则在三种滤波器上都保持了高分,带通 R² 达到 0.8206。作者指出,PPGN 之所以在带通上失手,正是因为它缺少 G2N2 那份能显式保留边信息的记忆。

zh.caption: 表3 频谱节点回归上的 R²(10 次运行中位数,越高越好)。PPGN 在带通滤波上失效,G2N2 三类滤波器均表现稳健。

zh.text: 哪些规则真的重要:文法约简消融
最能体现这套方法特色的,是围绕文法约简做的消融实验。作者在 QM9 的 R² 目标上,比较了完整文法 G(L3)、中间文法 i-G(L3) 与约简文法 r-G(L3):三者误差基本持平,说明约简只是去掉了冗余,没有动到表达力。但一旦越过约简文法、继续删掉核心规则,误差就会明显上升。
这种「退化」本身就是有用的信息:它量化了每条运算规则对性能的贡献。换句话说,当某个任务并不需要完整的 3-WL 表达力时,你可以照着这张图有依据地对模型做裁剪,而不是盲目地砍参数。

zh.caption: 图6 QM9 R² 上参数量与 MAE 的散点。完整文法 G(L3)、中间文法 i-G(L3)、约简文法 r-G(L3) 及其加入一条规则 (Mᵀ) 的变体误差相近;而从 r-G(L3) 中继续删去 {MM}、{M⊙M}、diag(Vc) 等核心规则(记作 \)后,MAE 明显抬高,验证了每条规则的作用。

zh.text: 小结:让表达力「与生俱来」
G2N2 真正改变的是工作流:不再是先设计网络、再祈祷能证明它足够强,而是从一个表达力已知的语言出发,约简成干净的文法,然后把网络直接从规则里读出来,表达力在构造时就有了保证。落到实处,就是一个可证明 3-WL、同时比前辈更快更准的模型。
更值得留意的是,这套「文法化」框架本身是通用的:原则上,任何一个代数语言的片段,都能沿同样的路径被转成一个继承其表达力的网络。G2N2 是这个想法的第一个具体产物,而它指向的方向,是一整类「按需定制表达力」的图神经网络设计方法。

zh.subtitle: 法国 LITIS 与 LIFAT 实验室提出 G2N2:用上下文无关文法从矩阵语言直接推导出可证明 3-WL 的图神经网络

en.text: Step one: from a language to a grammar, then to a reduced grammar

The derivation begins from a set of operations: L3 = {· (matrix product), ᵀ (transpose), 1 (the all-ones vector), diag (take the diagonal), ⊙ (element-wise product)}. The authors first write an exhaustive context-free grammar G(L3) whose generated sentences are exactly the fragment ML(L3). This step turns "a language" into "a set of production rules."

Then comes the key move: reduction. While proving at every step that no 3-WL expressiveness is lost, they strip away redundant rules and variables until only the essential core productions remain: the reduced grammar r-G(L3). Reduction both makes the eventual network leaner and, as a bonus, reveals which operations actually matter. To see how a rule becomes a computation, look at one iteration of the procedure below.

en.caption: Figure 2. One iteration in four steps. (1) Rule selection: pick a production from (M⊙M), (MM), diag(Vc), (MVc). (2) Input selection: fetch the operands that rule needs from the matrix memory and vector memory. (3) Rule computation: apply the operation (here, A⊙A²). (4) Output storage: write the result back into the matching memory. Iterating this loop gradually accumulates richer graph features in memory.

zh.caption: 图1 G2N2 的整条推导流水线。从与 3-WL 等价的矩阵语言片段 ML(L3) 出发,先写出穷尽的上下文无关文法 G(L3),再约简为紧凑的 r-G(L3),最后把约简文法里存活下来的变量当作网络输入、产生式规则当作层内运算,直接得到 G2N2 的一层。

zh.text: 背景:从 WL 层级到矩阵语言
这套方法的起点,是一个漂亮的观察:1-WL 与 3-WL 测试都可以改写成一种矩阵语言 MATLANG 的片段。具体地说,两张图在 3-WL 看来一样,当且仅当片段 ML(L3) 里你能写出的每一个「句子」在两张图上取值都相同。这在组合数学(WL 测试)和线性代数(矩阵运算)之间架起了一座桥。
但桥不等于路。把这样一个片段变成真正可训练的网络,此前只能一个个手工来做,得到的模型往往拿不到完整的 3-WL 保证。例如同样从 MATLANG 视角出发的 GNNML3,只被证明比 1-WL 更强,而没能证到 3-WL,原因恰恰是缺少一条系统化的推导路径。G2N2 要做的,就是把这条路一次性铺好。

最能体现这套方法特色的,是围绕文法约简做的消融实验。作者在 QM9 的 R² 目标上,比较了完整文法 G(L3)、中间文法 i-G(L3) 与约简文法 r-G(L3):三者误差基本持平,说明约简只是去掉了冗余,没有动到表达力。但一旦越过约简文法、继续删掉核心规则,误差就会明显上升。

en.text: Classification and a spectral stress test

The second arena is the classic TUD graph-classification benchmark, spanning molecular graphs like MUTAG and PTC and social graphs like IMDB. G2N2 beats the second-best GNN competitor on five of the six datasets, and ranks first outright on MUTAG, PTC, and Proteins.

en.caption: Table 2. TUD results comparing G2N2 with the strongest GNN competitor (accuracy, higher is better; G2N2's rank among GNNs in parentheses). Full results are in the paper's Table 6.

en.text: The third arena is closer to a stress test: learning spectral filters on 900-node graphs. Message-passing networks are known to behave like low-pass filters by default, so high-pass and especially band-pass filtering is where expressiveness really shows. The result is telling. PPGN nearly maxes out low-pass and high-pass but collapses on band-pass (R² of just 0.1041), whereas G2N2 stays strong across all three, reaching a band-pass R² of 0.8206. The authors argue PPGN fails here precisely because it lacks the kind of explicit edge memory that G2N2 keeps.

en.caption: Table 3. R² on spectral node regression (median of 10 runs, higher is better). PPGN fails on band-pass filtering; G2N2 remains robust across all three filter types.

en.text: Which rules matter: the grammar-reduction ablation

The experiment that best captures the method's flavor is the ablation around grammar reduction. On the QM9 R² target, the authors compare the full grammar G(L3), an intermediate grammar i-G(L3), and the reduced grammar r-G(L3): their errors are essentially the same, confirming that reduction only removes redundancy and leaves expressiveness untouched. But once you push past the reduced grammar and start deleting core rules, the error climbs noticeably.

That degradation is itself useful information: it quantifies how much each operation contributes to the final accuracy. In other words, when a task does not actually need the full 3-WL power, this plot tells you which rules you can safely drop, so you can prune the model deliberately instead of hacking away at parameters and hoping accuracy survives.

en.caption: Figure 6. Parameter count versus MAE on QM9's R² target. The full grammar G(L3), the intermediate i-G(L3), the reduced r-G(L3), and a variant adding one rule (Mᵀ) all land at comparable error; removing core rules such as {MM}, {M⊙M}, or diag(Vc) from r-G(L3) (marked with \) drives MAE up, confirming each rule pulls its weight.

zh.text: 衡量一个图神经网络（GNN）到底有多「聪明」，业界最常用的标尺是 Weisfeiler-Lehman（WL）层级：如果两张不同构的图连 k 阶 WL 测试都分不开，那么再强的 GNN 也分不开。于是多年来的惯例是,先凭直觉设计一个模型,再回过头去证明它能匹配某一阶 WL 测试。表达力的保证,总是作为「事后」的一纸证明补上来的。
问题在于,这条路没有通用配方。每设计一个新架构,就要重新写一遍表达力证明;而反过来的方向,也就是「给定一个已知表达力的数学片段,机械地造出一个继承其表达力的网络」,一直没有系统方法。已有的 3-WL 模型也各有短板:3-IGN 的算子基规模随 2k 阶 Bell 数爆炸,内存吃紧;PPGN 虽然可算,却只被证明能模拟 2-FWL,与语言表达力之间没有构造性的桥梁。
ICLR 2024 上的这篇 G2N2 反其道而行:它不再「先设计后证明」,而是「先选定一个表达力已知的语言片段,再把它的规则直接读成网络的层」。整条流水线是自动的,产出的网络可证明达到 3-WL 表达力,而且在实验里比现有 3-WL 模型更快、更准。下图是全文的一张总览。

zh.caption: 图1 G2N2 的整条推导流水线。从与 3-WL 等价的矩阵语言片段 ML(L3) 出发,先写出穷尽的上下文无关文法 G(L3),再约简为紧凑的 r-G(L3),最后把约简文法里存活下来的变量当作网络输入、产生式规则当作层内运算,直接得到 G2N2 的一层。

zh.subtitle: 法国 LITIS 与 LIFAT 实验室提出 G2N2:用上下文无关文法从矩阵语言直接推导出可证明 3-WL 的图神经网络

en.text: The standard ruler for how much a graph neural network (GNN) can tell apart is the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) hierarchy: if two non-isomorphic graphs already look identical to the k-th-order WL test, no GNN in that class will separate them either. For years the field has worked in one direction only. You design a model on intuition, then go back and prove it matches, say, the third-order test. The expressiveness guarantee always arrives afterward, as a separate proof stapled onto the architecture.

The trouble is that there is no general recipe for that. Every new architecture needs its own bespoke expressiveness proof, and the reverse direction, starting from a mathematical object whose power you already know and mechanically building a network that inherits it, has been missing. Existing 3-WL models each pay a price: 3-IGN's operator basis grows like the 2k-th Bell number and is memory-hungry, while PPGN is tractable but was only shown to mimic 2-FWL, with no constructive bridge from a language to the model.

This ICLR 2024 paper, G2N2, runs the process the other way. Instead of "design first, prove later," it picks a language fragment whose expressiveness is already known, then reads the network's layers straight off that fragment's rules. The whole pipeline is automatic, the resulting network is provably 3-WL, and in practice it turns out faster and more accurate than the existing 3-WL models. The figure below is the whole paper in one picture.

en.caption: Figure 1. The full G2N2 derivation pipeline. Starting from the matrix-language fragment ML(L3), which is equivalent in power to the 3-WL test, the authors write an exhaustive context-free grammar G(L3), reduce it to the compact r-G(L3), and then read a G2N2 layer directly off the reduced grammar: surviving variables become the network's inputs and production rules become the layer's operations.

zh.caption: 图6 QM9 R² 上参数量与 MAE 的散点。完整文法 G(L3)、中间文法 i-G(L3)、约简文法 r-G(L3) 及其加入一条规则 (Mᵀ) 的变体误差相近;而从 r-G(L3) 中继续删去 {MM}、{M⊙M}、diag(Vc) 等核心规则(记作 \)后,MAE 明显抬高,验证了每条规则的作用。

en.title: ICLR 2024 | Stop Proving Expressiveness After the Fact, Build It In
en.subtitle: G2N2, from the LITIS and LIFAT labs in France, turns a matrix-language fragment into a provably 3-WL graph neural network by way of a context-free grammar

zh.title: ICLR 2024 | 别再事后证明了：把表达力「写」进图神经网络
zh.subtitle: 法国 LITIS 与 LIFAT 实验室提出 G2N2:用上下文无关文法从矩阵语言直接推导出可证明 3-WL 的图神经网络

en.text: The standard ruler for how much a graph neural network (GNN) can tell apart is the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) hierarchy: if two non-isomorphic graphs already look identical to the k-th-order WL test, no GNN in that class will separate them either. For years the field has worked in one direction only. You design a model on intuition, then go back and prove it matches, say, the third-order test. The expressiveness guarantee always arrives afterward, as a separate proof stapled onto the architecture.

The trouble is that there is no general recipe for that. Every new architecture needs its own bespoke expressiveness proof, and the reverse direction, starting from a mathematical object whose power you already know and mechanically building a network that inherits it, has been missing. Existing 3-WL models each pay a price: 3-IGN's operator basis grows like the 2k-th Bell number and is memory-hungry, while PPGN is tractable but was only shown to mimic 2-FWL, with no constructive bridge from a language to the model.

This ICLR 2024 paper, G2N2, runs the process the other way. Instead of "design first, prove later," it picks a language fragment whose expressiveness is already known, then reads the network's layers straight off that fragment's rules. The whole pipeline is automatic, the resulting network is provably 3-WL, and in practice it turns out faster and more accurate than the existing 3-WL models. The figure below is the whole paper in one picture.

en.caption: Figure 1. The full G2N2 derivation pipeline. Starting from the matrix-language fragment ML(L3), which is equivalent in power to the 3-WL test, the authors write an exhaustive context-free grammar G(L3), reduce it to the compact r-G(L3), and then read a G2N2 layer directly off the reduced grammar: surviving variables become the network's inputs and production rules become the layer's operations.

en.text: Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.01590    Code: https://github.com/JPiquenot/Wesfeiler-and-Lehman-go-grammatical

zh.caption: 图1 G2N2 的整条推导流水线。从与 3-WL 等价的矩阵语言片段 ML(L3) 出发,先写出穷尽的上下文无关文法 G(L3),再约简为紧凑的 r-G(L3),最后把约简文法里存活下来的变量当作网络输入、产生式规则当作层内运算,直接得到 G2N2 的一层。

zh.text: 小结:让表达力「与生俱来」
G2N2 真正改变的是工作流:不再是先设计网络、再祈祷能证明它足够强,而是从一个表达力已知的语言出发,约简成干净的文法,然后把网络直接从规则里读出来,表达力在构造时就有了保证。落到实处,就是一个可证明 3-WL、同时比前辈更快更准的模型。
更值得留意的是,这套「文法化」框架本身是通用的:原则上,任何一个代数语言的片段,都能沿同样的路径被转成一个继承其表达力的网络。G2N2 是这个想法的第一个具体产物,而它指向的方向,是一整类「按需定制表达力」的图神经网络设计方法。

Takeaway: expressiveness by construction

What G2N2 really changes is the workflow. G2N2 is the first concrete instance of that idea, and it points toward a whole family of GNN designs where you choose the expressiveness you want up front and build the model to match.
